work.title: The Second Part of King Henry the Fourth
work.author: William Shakespeare

content.text: Enter Falstaff, with his Page bearing his sword and buckler.

lines.text: Sirrah, you giant, what says the doctor to my water?
lines.plainText: Sirrah you giant what says the doctor to my water

lines.text: He said, sir, the water itself was a good healthy water; but, for the party that owed it, he might have moe diseases than he knew for.
lines.plainText: He said sir the water itself was a good healthy water but for the party that owed it he might have moe diseases than he knew for

lines.text: Men of all sorts take a pride to gird at me. The brain of this foolish-compounded clay, man, is not able to invent anything that tends to laughter more than I invent, or is invented on me. I am not only witty in myself, but the cause that wit is in other men. I do here walk before thee like a sow that hath overwhelmed all her litter but one. If the Prince put thee into my service for any other reason than to set me off, why then I have no judgement. Thou whoreson mandrake, thou art fitter to be worn in my cap than to wait at my heels. I was never manned with an agate till now, but I will inset you neither in gold nor silver, but in vile apparel, and send you back again to your master, for a jewel,—the juvenal, the Prince your master, whose chin is not yet fledge. I will sooner have a beard grow in the palm of my hand than he shall get one off his cheek; and yet he will not stick to say his face is a face-royal. God may finish it when He will, 'tis not a hair amiss yet. He may keep it still at a face-royal, for a barber shall never earn sixpence out of it. And yet he'll be crowing as if he had writ man ever since his father was a bachelor. He may keep his own grace, but he's almost out of mine, I can assure him. What said Master Dommelton about the satin for my short cloak and my slops?

lines.text: He said, sir, you should procure him better assurance than Bardolph. He would not take his band and yours, he liked not the security.
lines.plainText: He said sir you should procure him better assurance than Bardolph He would not take his band and yours he liked not the security

lines.text: Let him be damned like the glutton! Pray God his tongue be hotter! A whoreson Achitophel! A rascally yea-forsooth knave, to bear a gentleman in hand, and then stand upon security! The whoreson smooth-pates do now wear nothing but high shoes and bunches of keys at their girdles; and if a man is through with them in honest taking up, then they must stand upon security. I had as lief they would put ratsbane in my mouth as offer to stop it with security. I looked he should have sent me two and twenty yards of satin, as I am a true knight, and he sends me "security". Well, he may sleep in security, for he hath the horn of abundance, and the lightness of his wife shines through it; and yet cannot he see, though he have his own lanthorn to light him. Where's Bardolph?

lines.text: He's gone into Smithfield to buy your worship a horse.
lines.plainText: He's gone into Smithfield to buy your worship a horse

lines.text: I bought him in Paul's, and he'll buy me a horse in Smithfield. An I could get me but a wife in the stews, I were manned, horsed, and wived.

content.text: Enter the Lord Chief Justice and Servant.

lines.text: Sir, here comes the nobleman that committed the Prince for striking him about Bardolph.
lines.plainText: Sir here comes the nobleman that committed the Prince for striking him about Bardolph

lines.text: Wait close, I will not see him.
lines.plainText: Wait close I will not see him

lines.text: What's he that goes there?
lines.plainText: What's he that goes there

lines.text: Falstaff, an 't please your lordship.
lines.plainText: Falstaff an 't please your lordship

lines.text: He that was in question for the robbery?
lines.plainText: He that was in question for the robbery

lines.text: He, my lord; but he hath since done good service at Shrewsbury, and, as I hear, is now going with some charge to the Lord John of Lancaster.
lines.plainText: He my lord but he hath since done good service at Shrewsbury and as I hear is now going with some charge to the Lord John of Lancaster

lines.text: What, to York? Call him back again.
lines.plainText: What to York Call him back again

lines.text: Sir John Falstaff!
lines.plainText: Sir John Falstaff

lines.text: Boy, tell him I am deaf.
lines.plainText: Boy tell him I am deaf

lines.text: You must speak louder, my master is deaf.
lines.plainText: You must speak louder my master is deaf

lines.text: I am sure he is, to the hearing of anything good.
lines.plainText: I am sure he is to the hearing of anything good

lines.text: Go pluck him by the elbow, I must speak with him.
lines.plainText: Go pluck him by the elbow I must speak with him

lines.text: Sir John!
lines.plainText: Sir John

lines.text: What! A young knave, and begging! Is there not wars? Is there not employment? Doth not the King lack subjects? Do not the rebels need soldiers? Though it be a shame to be on any side but one, it is worse shame to beg than to be on the worst side, were it worse than the name of rebellion can tell how to make it.
lines.plainText: What A young knave and begging Is there not wars Is there not employment Doth not the King lack subjects Do not the rebels need soldiers Though it be a shame to be on any side but one it is worse shame to beg than to be on the worst side were it worse than the name of rebellion can tell how to make it

lines.text: You mistake me, sir.
lines.plainText: You mistake me sir

lines.text: Why, sir, did I say you were an honest man? Setting my knighthood and my soldiership aside, I had lied in my throat if I had said so.
lines.plainText: Why sir did I say you were an honest man Setting my knighthood and my soldiership aside I had lied in my throat if I had said so

lines.text: I pray you, sir, then set your knighthood and your soldiership aside, and give me leave to tell you, you lie in your throat, if you say I am any other than an honest man.
lines.plainText: I pray you sir then set your knighthood and your soldiership aside and give me leave to tell you you lie in your throat if you say I am any other than an honest man

lines.text: I give thee leave to tell me so? I lay aside that which grows to me? If thou get'st any leave of me, hang me; if thou tak'st leave, thou wert better be hanged. You hunt counter. Hence! Avaunt!
lines.plainText: I give thee leave to tell me so I lay aside that which grows to me If thou get'st any leave of me hang me if thou tak'st leave thou wert better be hanged You hunt counter Hence Avaunt

lines.text: Sir, my lord would speak with you.
lines.plainText: Sir my lord would speak with you

lines.text: Sir John Falstaff, a word with you.
lines.plainText: Sir John Falstaff a word with you

lines.text: My good lord! God give your lordship good time of day. I am glad to see your lordship abroad. I heard say your lordship was sick. I hope your lordship goes abroad by advice. Your lordship, though not clean past your youth, hath yet some smack of age in you, some relish of the saltness of time; and I most humbly beseech your lordship to have a reverend care of your health.

lines.text: Sir John, I sent for you before your expedition to Shrewsbury.
lines.plainText: Sir John I sent for you before your expedition to Shrewsbury

lines.text: An 't please your lordship, I hear his Majesty is returned with some discomfort from Wales.
lines.plainText: An 't please your lordship I hear his Majesty is returned with some discomfort from Wales

lines.text: I talk not of his Majesty. You would not come when I sent for you.
lines.plainText: I talk not of his Majesty You would not come when I sent for you

lines.text: And I hear, moreover, his Highness is fallen into this same whoreson apoplexy.
lines.plainText: And I hear moreover his Highness is fallen into this same whoreson apoplexy

lines.text: Well, God mend him! I pray you let me speak with you.
lines.plainText: Well God mend him I pray you let me speak with you

lines.text: This apoplexy, as I take it, is a kind of lethargy, an 't please your lordship, a kind of sleeping in the blood, a whoreson tingling.
lines.plainText: This apoplexy as I take it is a kind of lethargy an 't please your lordship a kind of sleeping in the blood a whoreson tingling

lines.text: What tell you me of it? Be it as it is.
lines.plainText: What tell you me of it Be it as it is

lines.text: It hath it original from much grief, from study and perturbation of the brain. I have read the cause of his effects in Galen. It is a kind of deafness.
lines.plainText: It hath it original from much grief from study and perturbation of the brain I have read the cause of his effects in Galen It is a kind of deafness

lines.text: I think you are fallen into the disease, for you hear not what I say to you.
lines.plainText: I think you are fallen into the disease for you hear not what I say to you

lines.text: Very well, my lord, very well. Rather, an 't please you, it is the disease of not listening, the malady of not marking, that I am troubled withal.
lines.plainText: Very well my lord very well Rather an 't please you it is the disease of not listening the malady of not marking that I am troubled withal

lines.text: To punish you by the heels would amend the attention of your ears, and I care not if I do become your physician.
lines.plainText: To punish you by the heels would amend the attention of your ears and I care not if I do become your physician

lines.text: I am as poor as Job, my lord, but not so patient. Your lordship may minister the potion of imprisonment to me in respect of poverty; but how I should be your patient to follow your prescriptions, the wise may make some dram of a scruple, or indeed a scruple itself.
lines.plainText: I am as poor as Job my lord but not so patient Your lordship may minister the potion of imprisonment to me in respect of poverty but how I should be your patient to follow your prescriptions the wise may make some dram of a scruple or indeed a scruple itself

lines.text: I sent for you, when there were matters against you for your life, to come speak with me.
lines.plainText: I sent for you when there were matters against you for your life to come speak with me

lines.text: As I was then advised by my learned counsel in the laws of this land-service, I did not come.
lines.plainText: As I was then advised by my learned counsel in the laws of this landservice I did not come

lines.text: Well, the truth is, Sir John, you live in great infamy.
lines.plainText: Well the truth is Sir John you live in great infamy

lines.text: He that buckles himself in my belt cannot live in less.
lines.plainText: He that buckles himself in my belt cannot live in less

lines.text: Your means are very slender, and your waste is great.
lines.plainText: Your means are very slender and your waste is great

lines.text: I would it were otherwise, I would my means were greater and my waist slenderer.
lines.plainText: I would it were otherwise I would my means were greater and my waist slenderer

lines.text: You have misled the youthful prince.
lines.plainText: You have misled the youthful prince

lines.text: The young prince hath misled me. I am the fellow with the great belly, and he my dog.
lines.plainText: The young prince hath misled me I am the fellow with the great belly and he my dog

lines.text: Well, I am loath to gall a new-healed wound. Your day's service at Shrewsbury hath a little gilded over your night's exploit on Gad's Hill. You may thank th' unquiet time for your quiet o'er-posting that action.
lines.plainText: Well I am loath to gall a newhealed wound Your day's service at Shrewsbury hath a little gilded over your night's exploit on Gad's Hill You may thank th' unquiet time for your quiet o'erposting that action

lines.text: My lord!
lines.plainText: My lord

lines.text: But since all is well, keep it so: wake not a sleeping wolf.
lines.plainText: But since all is well keep it so wake not a sleeping wolf

lines.text: To wake a wolf is as bad as smell a fox.
lines.plainText: To wake a wolf is as bad as smell a fox

lines.text: What! You are as a candle, the better part burnt out.
lines.plainText: What You are as a candle the better part burnt out

lines.text: A wassail candle, my lord, all tallow. If I did say of wax, my growth would approve the truth.
lines.plainText: A wassail candle my lord all tallow If I did say of wax my growth would approve the truth

lines.text: There is not a white hair in your face but should have his effect of gravity.
lines.plainText: There is not a white hair in your face but should have his effect of gravity

lines.text: His effect of gravy, gravy, gravy.
lines.plainText: His effect of gravy gravy gravy

lines.text: You follow the young prince up and down, like his ill angel.
lines.plainText: You follow the young prince up and down like his ill angel

lines.text: Not so, my lord, your ill angel is light, but I hope he that looks upon me will take me without weighing. And yet in some respects, I grant, I cannot go. I cannot tell. Virtue is of so little regard in these costermongers' times that true valour is turned bearherd; pregnancy is made a tapster, and hath his quick wit wasted in giving reckonings. All the other gifts appertinent to man, as the malice of this age shapes them, are not worth a gooseberry. You that are old consider not the capacities of us that are young; you do measure the heat of our livers with the bitterness of your galls, and we that are in the vaward of our youth, I must confess, are wags too.
lines.plainText: Not so my lord your ill angel is light but I hope he that looks upon me will take me without weighing And yet in some respects I grant I cannot go I cannot tell Virtue is of so little regard in these costermongers' times that true valour is turned bearherd pregnancy is made a tapster and hath his quick wit wasted in giving reckonings All the other gifts appertinent to man as the malice of this age shapes them are not worth a gooseberry You that are old consider not the capacities of us that are young you do measure the heat of our livers with the bitterness of your galls and we that are in the vaward of our youth I must confess are wags too

lines.text: Do you set down your name in the scroll of youth, that are written down old with all the characters of age? Have you not a moist eye, a dry hand, a yellow cheek, a white beard, a decreasing leg, an increasing belly? Is not your voice broken, your wind short, your chin double, your wit single, and every part about you blasted with antiquity? And will you yet call yourself young? Fie, fie, fie, Sir John!
lines.plainText: Do you set down your name in the scroll of youth that are written down old with all the characters of age Have you not a moist eye a dry hand a yellow cheek a white beard a decreasing leg an increasing belly Is not your voice broken your wind short your chin double your wit single and every part about you blasted with antiquity And will you yet call yourself young Fie fie fie Sir John

lines.text: My lord, I was born about three of the clock in the afternoon, with a white head and something a round belly. For my voice, I have lost it with halloing and singing of anthems. To approve my youth further, I will not. The truth is, I am only old in judgement and understanding; and he that will caper with me for a thousand marks, let him lend me the money, and have at him! For the box of the ear that the Prince gave you, he gave it like a rude prince, and you took it like a sensible lord. I have checked him for it, and the young lion repents. Marry, not in ashes and sackcloth, but in new silk and old sack.

lines.text: Well, God send the Prince a better companion!
lines.plainText: Well God send the Prince a better companion

lines.text: God send the companion a better prince! I cannot rid my hands of him.
lines.plainText: God send the companion a better prince I cannot rid my hands of him

lines.text: Well, the King hath severed you and Prince Harry. I hear you are going with Lord John of Lancaster against the Archbishop and the Earl of Northumberland.
lines.plainText: Well the King hath severed you and Prince Harry I hear you are going with Lord John of Lancaster against the Archbishop and the Earl of Northumberland

lines.text: Yea, I thank your pretty sweet wit for it. But look you pray, all you that kiss my lady Peace at home, that our armies join not in a hot day; for, by the Lord, I take but two shirts out with me, and I mean not to sweat extraordinarily. If it be a hot day, and I brandish anything but a bottle, I would I might never spit white again. There is not a dangerous action can peep out his head but I am thrust upon it. Well, I cannot last ever. But it was alway yet the trick of our English nation, if they have a good thing, to make it too common. If ye will needs say I am an old man, you should give me rest. I would to God my name were not so terrible to the enemy as it is. I were better to be eaten to death with a rust than to be scoured to nothing with perpetual motion.

lines.text: Well, be honest, be honest, and God bless your expedition!
lines.plainText: Well be honest be honest and God bless your expedition

lines.text: Will your lordship lend me a thousand pound to furnish me forth?
lines.plainText: Will your lordship lend me a thousand pound to furnish me forth

lines.text: Not a penny, not a penny; you are too impatient to bear crosses. Fare you well: commend me to my cousin Westmoreland.
lines.plainText: Not a penny not a penny you are too impatient to bear crosses Fare you well commend me to my cousin Westmoreland

lines.text: If I do, fillip me with a three-man beetle. A man can no more separate age and covetousness than he can part young limbs and lechery: but the gout galls the one, and the pox pinches the other; and so both the degrees prevent my curses. Boy!
lines.plainText: If I do fillip me with a threeman beetle A man can no more separate age and covetousness than he can part young limbs and lechery but the gout galls the one and the pox pinches the other and so both the degrees prevent my curses Boy

lines.text: Sir?
lines.plainText: Sir

lines.text: What money is in my purse?
lines.plainText: What money is in my purse

lines.text: Seven groats and two pence.
lines.plainText: Seven groats and two pence

lines.text: I can get no remedy against this consumption of the purse. Borrowing only lingers and lingers it out, but the disease is incurable. Go bear this letter to my Lord of Lancaster; this to the Prince; this to the Earl of Westmoreland; and this to old Mistress Ursula, whom I have weekly sworn to marry since I perceived the first white hair of my chin. About it. You know where to find me. [Exit Page.] A pox of this gout! or a gout of this pox! for the one or the other plays the rogue with my great toe. 'Tis no matter if I do halt; I have the wars for my colour, and my pension shall seem the more reasonable. A good wit will make use of anything. I will turn diseases to commodity.
